variables.q: What is the difference between var, let, and const, and when would you use each?
variables.what:
JavaScript gives you three ways to declare a variable. They differ in scope, hoisting, and whether you can reassign them.

var is the old style: it is visible throughout the whole function. let and const are the modern style: they are visible only inside their own { } block.
variables.why: var had two problems. It leaked out of if and for blocks, and it allowed redeclaration, which could silently wipe out an earlier value. let and const fix both.
pros: const signals that the binding will not be reassigned.
Block scope stops variables from leaking out.
Redeclaring a name is an error, so you can't overwrite a value by accident.
cons: const does not make an object immutable. This is the most common misconception.
Because of the TDZ, using a variable before its declaration throws an error (which is actually a good thing).
Older browsers need transpiling to support let/const.
gotchas: After const arr = [], arr.push(1) still works. const only prevents reassignment.
A hoisted var is undefined until its assignment runs, while a let read before its declaration throws an error.
At the global level, var x becomes window.x, but let x does not.
terms: The region of code where a variable is visible.
Giving an existing variable a new value.
Declaring a variable again with the same name in the same scope.
where: Start with const. Switch to let only when you must reassign. Don't use var.
for (let i...) creates a fresh i on every iteration, so closures capture the right value.
Older codebases still use var, so you need to recognize the bugs its leaking causes.
variables.visualCap: var is visible across the whole function; let and const stay inside their own block.

hoisting.desc: Before execution, JS moves declarations (not initializations) to the top of their scope.
hoisting.qsub: What is the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)?
hoisting.what:
Before your code runs, JS scans the whole scope once and registers every declaration. The value, however, is only assigned when execution reaches that line.

That is why reading a var before its declaration gives undefined: the variable exists, but nothing has been assigned to it yet.
hoisting.analogy: Think of a class attendance register. Every name is written in before the lesson starts (the declaration), but students walk in at different times. A name in the register is the declaration; a student who hasn't arrived yet is the value undefined.
hoisting.why: A hoisted var reads as undefined, which created silent bugs: the code ran but gave wrong results. So let and const introduced the TDZ: accessing them before their declaration throws an error. The bug shows up immediately instead of hiding.
pros: Function declarations can be written below the code that calls them.
The TDZ turns hidden mistakes into immediate errors.
You don't have to order helper functions before their first use.
cons: A hoisted var reads as undefined, which causes silent bugs.
Arrow functions and function expressions are not hoisted like declarations, which confuses many people.
The behavior feels counter-intuitive to beginners.
gotchas: Only the declaration is hoisted, not the assignment. That is the core idea.
function f(){} is hoisted completely, but var f = function(){} hoists only the var f part.
class declarations are also in the TDZ, so you can't use new on a class before its declaration.
terms: Before execution, JS registers all declarations at the top of their scope, but not their values.
Temporal Dead Zone: the stretch from the start of a block until a let/const declaration, during which the variable cannot be accessed.
where: When you ask "where did this undefined come from?", hoisting is often the answer.
You can write a function declaration lower down and still call it above. This is common for helper functions.
The TDZ and "what is hoisted and what is not" come up directly.
hoisting.visualCap: All three are hoisted, but differently: var starts as undefined, let/const sit in the TDZ, and function declarations are fully ready.

datatypes.q: What is the difference between primitive and reference types in JavaScript?
datatypes.what:
A primitive variable holds the value itself. When you copy it, you get a new, independent value.

A reference variable holds only an address. The actual object lives elsewhere (in the heap). When you copy it, the address is copied, not the object. Two names, one house.
datatypes.analogy:
A primitive is like handing someone a photocopy. If they tear up their copy, yours is safe.
A reference is like giving someone your house address. If they go and paint the wall, your house gets painted too.
datatypes.why: Many JavaScript bugs come from this: "I made a copy, so why did the original change?" It is also why === returns false for two similar-looking objects: it compares addresses, not contents.
pros: Passing a large object by reference is cheap, because the data isn't copied.
Change it in one place and every holder sees the update (when that is what you want).
Primitives are always safe to copy, since each copy is independent.
cons: The original can change unintentionally. This is the most common source of JS state bugs.
=== can't tell you whether two objects have the same contents.
You have to understand the difference between shallow and deep copies.
gotchas: [...arr] and {...obj} are shallow copies: they copy only the first level.
Avoid JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) for deep copies: Dates become strings and undefined values disappear. Prefer structuredClone.
typeof null returns "object". It is a long-standing bug in JavaScript that was never fixed.
terms: A simple value: number, string, boolean, null, undefined, symbol, or bigint.
An object, array, or function. The variable stores a reference (address) to it, not the value itself.
where: "I copied it, so why did the original change?" is the cause of most state bugs.
State must be updated immutably. Otherwise React doesn't detect the change.
You can't compare objects by content with ===. You need a deep comparison.
datatypes.visualCap: Copying a primitive creates a new value. Copying an object copies only the address, so both names point to the same house.

coercion.what:
When you combine two different types, JS tries to convert them to a common type, whether or not that makes sense.

Remember two rules: + leans toward strings (if either operand is a string, it concatenates instead of adding), and all other arithmetic operators lean toward numbers.
coercion.why: JS was designed as a language that tries never to crash, so it will run even questionable code. That makes quick scripts easy to write, but the downside is that bugs don't crash; they silently produce wrong results.
pros: Quick scripts are easy to write, with no type ceremony.
You can write short checks like if (arr.length).
Template literals turn everything into a string automatically.
cons: Bugs don't crash; they silently produce wrong results.
You have to memorize the rules, because guessing doesn't work.
Without TypeScript, many of these mistakes go uncaught.

You didn't ask for it; JS did it on its own, as in "5" * 2.

=== is straightforward: it is true only if the types match and the values match.

== first coerces the operands to a common type, then compares. That "coerce first" step is where everything goes wrong.
equality.why: There is really only one place where == is useful: x == null, which catches both null and undefined in one check. Use === everywhere else.

x == null is a handy shortcut.
Object.is handles the NaN and -0 edge cases correctly.

nullish.q: What is the difference between null, undefined, and NaN? How do you reliably check for each?
nullish.what:
All three look like "nothing", but their meaning is different:

undefined = "no value was ever given". null = "deliberately left empty". NaN = "tried to produce a number and failed".
nullish.analogy: Picture a form field. undefined: the field was never shown. null: the field was shown and the user entered "N/A". NaN: the user typed "abc" for age.
nullish.why: The difference matters because undefined is often a bug ("no value arrived") while null is often valid ("empty is fine"). The same applies in API design: returning null means "I looked and found nothing", while undefined suggests "maybe I never looked".
pros: ?? and ?. make this whole area much easier.
Two distinct meanings make the intent of the code clearer.
x == null checks for both at once.
cons: typeof null returning "object" still confuses people.
Having two "empty" values is widely considered a design flaw.
NaN is not equal to itself.
gotchas: || vs ??: || falls back for every falsy value, while ?? falls back only for null/undefined.
typeof null === "object", so to detect null, write x === null.
A function with no return returns undefined, not null.
terms: No value was given. JavaScript assigns it automatically.
Not a Number: a numeric operation failed.
where: Use ??, not ||, or 0 and "" will be replaced too.
A field that is null means "empty"; undefined means "not present".
obj?.a?.b avoids crashes without a long chain of if checks.

scope.q: Explain the three types of scope in JavaScript, with examples.
scope.what:
There are three kinds of scope: global (the whole file), function (inside a function), and block (inside a { }, which applies only to let/const).

When JavaScript needs a variable, it searches from the inside out: first the current scope, then the next one out, all the way up to global. This is called the scope chain.
scope.analogy: Think of looking for something at home: first in your own room, then in the hall, then in the rest of the house. The search never goes the other way. Someone standing in the hall can't open the cupboard in your room.
scope.why: Without scope, every variable would be global, and variables from different functions would clash. Scope is also what makes closures possible, and ideas like this, hoisting, and the module pattern build on it.
pros: Variables don't clash, because each function has its own scope.
Block scope keeps for loop and if variables from leaking out.
The global namespace stays clean.
cons: In deeply nested code, it is hard to tell where a variable came from.
A long scope chain makes lookups slightly slower (negligible in practice).
The function scope of var still causes confusion in legacy code.
gotchas: Lexical means scope is decided by where the code is written, not where it is called.
var ignores block scope: it is visible throughout the entire function, even from outside the if it was declared in.
Assigning to a name without let/const/var creates a global variable (an error in strict mode).
terms: The region of code where a variable is visible.
If a variable isn't found, JS searches the outer scopes, up to global.
Scope is decided by where the code is written, not where it runs.
where: A closure captures the whole scope chain, so closures don't make sense without scope.
Different functions can use the same variable name without conflict.
Wrapping code in a function keeps the global scope clean.
scope.visualCap: Lookup always goes from inner to outer, never the reverse. So inner scopes can see outer ones, but outer scopes can't see inner ones.

closures.qsub: How does the classic loop-with-setTimeout bug demonstrate closures, and how do you fix it?
closures.what:
When you create a function inside another function, the inner one can see the outer function's variables. That part is normal.

The remarkable part is that even after the outer function has finished, the inner function still remembers those variables. They don't disappear. That is a closure.
closures.analogy: Imagine leaving the office for the day and packing a file into your bag. The office closes, but the file is still in your bag. The function is you, and the bag is the closure.
closures.why: JavaScript has no built-in private for plain functions, so how do you create data that only certain functions can access? Closures are the answer: keep the variable inside, and expose only the functions that need it.
pros: True private data, which had no other solution in old JS.
Each call gets its own bag, so two counters never interfere.
Removes the need for global variables.
cons: Memory is not released while the closure is still reachable.
The classic bug with loops and var (see below).
Deep nesting can be hard to read.
gotchas: for (var i=0;i<3;i++) setTimeout(()=>log(i)) prints 3 three times, because var gives you a single shared variable. Use let.
A closure doesn't keep a copy of the value; it keeps a reference to the variable, so it sees later changes.
In an interview, don't stop at the definition. Give a real use case too (for example debounce or useState).
terms: The region where a variable is visible.
A function that remembers its outer variables even after the outer function has finished.
where: useState relies on closures, which is how each component remembers its own state.
The timer ID lives in the closure, so every debounced function has its own timer.
In the module pattern, secret can't be accessed from outside.
closures.visualCap: makeCounter finishes and its stack frame is removed, but count survives because the inner function still holds a reference to it.

execution-context.desc: JS creates an execution context for every function call, and the call stack tracks the current chain of calls.
execution-context.what:
Whenever a function runs, JS creates a new frame that holds the function's variables, its scope chain, and its this.

These frames are pushed onto a stack. The top frame is the one running. When it finishes, it is removed and the frame below it continues.
execution-context.analogy: Think of a stack of books on a table. You always add a new book on top and take one from the top. You can't pull one out of the middle.
execution-context.why: The stack trace you see in an error is this same stack. And "Maximum call stack size exceeded" means the stack grew too tall and overflowed (usually infinite recursion).
pros: The order of execution is always predictable, with no race conditions.
A stack trace takes you straight to the bug.
Memory is freed automatically when a frame is removed.
cons: Deep recursion causes a stack overflow (around 10k calls).
A heavy function blocks the entire page.
Async code breaks the stack trace, which makes debugging harder.
gotchas: "Maximum call stack size exceeded" almost always means infinite recursion, so check your base case.
A stack trace reads backwards: the top line is the most recent call.
Replacing recursion with a loop removes the stack limit problem.
terms: A frame that records which code is running, what its variables are, and what this is.
The stack of these frames. The top one is the one currently running.
where: The "Call Stack" panel in DevTools shows exactly this, and it is the fastest way to find a bug.
Each recursive call creates a new frame, which is why there is a depth limit.
The event loop picks up new work only when this stack is empty.
execution-context.visualCap: Each function call creates a new frame. The top frame finishes first, which is why an error's stack trace reads backwards.

this.desc: this refers to the object that is executing the current function. Its value depends on how the function is called.
this.q: Explain how this is determined. What are the four binding rules?
this.what:
The value of this is not fixed when you write the function. It is determined when the function is called. That one sentence clears up most of the confusion.

The same function, called in different ways, can get a different this.
this.analogy: Think of the word "I". Who is speaking changes what it means, even though the word stays the same. this works the same way: its value depends on who is calling.
this.why: Thousands of objects can share the same method, since the method's code exists in just one place. So the method needs a way to know which object's data to use. That is what this provides.
pros: One method's code can be shared by thousands of objects.
Arrow functions have largely eliminated the callback this problem.
call/apply/bind give you full control over this.
cons: The value is decided at call time, so it is hard to predict just by reading the code.
When a method is assigned to a variable, this is lost.
Arrow and regular functions behave in opposite ways, which causes confusion.
gotchas: Arrow functions have no this of their own. They inherit it from where they are defined, so don't use an arrow function as an object method.
const fn = obj.method; fn() loses this. This is the most common bug.
In an interview, list the four rules (new → call/apply/bind → dot → standalone) to give the complete answer.
terms: The object the function is currently running on.
The place where the function is called. It determines this.
where: In React class components you had to bind this.handleClick, and this is why.
When you pass a method as a callback, this is lost. You need an arrow function or .bind().
In addEventListener, the this of a regular function is the element itself.
this.visualCap: Check from top to bottom: the first rule that matches decides this. Arrow functions are not on this list, because they inherit this from the surrounding scope.

arrow-fn.what:
Arrow functions are more than shorter syntax. They have no this of their own; they borrow this from the place where they are written.

That one difference decides when to use an arrow function and when not to.
arrow-fn.why: In the past, this got lost inside callbacks, so people wrote const self = this or used .bind(this). Arrow functions removed that hassle.

The short syntax keeps map/filter chains readable.
Implicit return makes one-line functions very concise.
cons: Wrong for object methods, because this does not point to the object.
Can't be used as a constructor, and has no arguments.

An arrow's this can't be changed with .call() or .bind().

hof.desc: Functions that take other functions as arguments or return them. They are the foundation of functional JS.
hof.what:
In JavaScript, a function is just a value. You can store it in a variable, pass it as an argument, or return it.

A function that takes another function or returns one is called a higher-order function. map, filter, setTimeout, and addEventListener are all examples.
hof.why: Without higher-order functions, you would write a full loop for every small task. They separate "what to do" from "how to iterate", which makes code shorter and more readable.
pros: Loop boilerplate disappears, so the intent is clear.
You can chain steps, and each step can be tested separately.
They are reusable: the same map works on any kind of data.
cons: Each step in a chain creates a new array, which uses extra memory on large data sets.
Too much chaining becomes hard to read.
A plain for loop is slightly faster on large data.
gotchas: map always returns a new array. Use forEach only for side effects.

currying.qsub: What is the difference between currying and partial application?
currying.what:
Turning add(a, b, c) into add(a)(b)(c) is called currying.

The benefit is that you can fill in some arguments ahead of time and get back a new, smaller function.
currying.analogy: Think of a tea order: "one tea, less sugar, with ginger". With currying, you state "less sugar, with ginger" once. After that, you only have to say "one tea".
currying.why: When the same setting keeps repeating, fill it in once and create a new function from it. This removes duplication.
pros: Fill in repeated arguments once.
Create small, specific functions and give them names.
Makes composition easier.
cons: f(a)(b)(c) looks odd and takes getting used to.
Each step creates a new function, which adds a bit of overhead.
Debugging is harder, because anonymous functions show up in the stack.
gotchas: Currying and partial application are not the same: currying always takes one argument at a time, while partial application can fix any number of arguments.
A simple wrapper function is often more readable than currying, so don't force it.

iife.desc: A function that runs the moment it is defined, used to create an isolated scope.
iife.qsub: How does an IIFE prevent polluting the global scope?
iife.what:
An IIFE is a function that runs immediately after it is defined: (function(){ ... })().

Its sole purpose was to create its own scope, so that its inner variables don't end up in the global scope.
iife.why:
Before let/const and ES modules, a function was the only way to create a scope. So developers wrapped entire files in one.

Today it is rarely needed, because block scope and modules do this job. But you'll still see it everywhere in old code and library bundles, so you need to recognize it.
pros: Keeps the global namespace clean.
A clean way to run one-time setup code.
Gives you private data via closure.
cons: Almost unnecessary today, since let, blocks, and modules are enough.
The syntax is heavy to read.
Unnamed functions show up as "anonymous" when debugging.
gotchas: If the previous line doesn't end with a semicolon, the IIFE's leading ( is parsed as a function call. This is a classic ASI bug.
You don't need IIFEs in new code. Saying so in an interview is a good signal.
An IIFE doesn't provide private data by itself. That comes from a closure. The IIFE only creates a scope.

A separate scope that keeps names from clashing in the global scope.
where: jQuery-era libraries were entirely wrapped in IIFEs.

call-apply-bind.q: What is the difference between call, apply, and bind? Implement bind from scratch.

All three exist for the same purpose: setting this manually.

call-apply-bind.why: You need these when this isn't automatically correct. The most common case is passing a method as a callback: this gets lost, and bind keeps it attached. Another case is borrowing a method from another object.
pros: Full control over this.
bind can also pre-fill arguments (partial application).
You can borrow a method from another object.

A bound function can't be re-bound to a different this.
None of them affect this in an arrow function.

memoization.what:
If a function is expensive and the same input keeps coming, recomputing it every time is wasteful.

event-loop.desc: The mechanism that keeps JS non-blocking: it takes tasks from the queues whenever the call stack is empty.
event-loop.q: Explain the event loop. What is the difference between the microtask queue and the macrotask queue?
event-loop.qsub: What is the output order for setTimeout, Promise.then, and queueMicrotask?
event-loop.what:
JS can do only one thing at a time. So why doesn't a 5-second network call freeze the page?

Because JS doesn't do that work itself. It hands it to the browser and moves on. When the response arrives, it goes into a queue. The event loop is the guard that keeps asking: "Is the stack empty? Then take the next item from the queue."
event-loop.analogy: A doctor (the stack) sees one patient at a time. She sends a blood sample to the lab and moves on to the next patient. When the report comes back, it joins a waiting line. And there are two lines: a VIP line (promises) and a normal line (setTimeout).
event-loop.why: Without it, every network call would freeze the whole page. It is also worth understanding because output-order interview questions and "why doesn't my state update show up immediately?" are both answered by it.
pros: The UI doesn't freeze even though JS is single-threaded.
No locks and far fewer race conditions, since only one piece of JS code runs at a time.
The ordering of promise callbacks is deterministic.
cons: A heavy calculation can freeze the entire page.
setTimeout(fn, 0) does not mean "right now".
The output order is confusing at first.
gotchas: setTimeout(fn, 0) doesn't run immediately. It is queued, and browsers may clamp it to about 4 ms.
Code after await runs as a microtask, so it runs before any waiting macrotask, such as a setTimeout callback.
In an interview, don't just say "it takes from the queue". Mention the two queues and their order.
terms: The stack of work currently executing, one frame at a time.
The normal queue: setTimeout, clicks, fetch responses.
The VIP queue: Promise.then and code after await.
where: Every frontend interview has an output-order question, and it follows exactly this rule.
"Why do I still see the old value right after setState?" Because React queues the update instead of applying it immediately.
A heavy loop keeps the stack busy, so the browser can't paint.
event-loop.visualCap: The key rule: after each macrotask, the microtask queue is drained completely, and only then does the next macrotask run.

callbacks.what:
When JavaScript has a slow task to do (a network request, a file read, a timer), it doesn't stop and wait. Instead, you hand it a function that says "run this when you're done". That function is a callback.

The trouble starts when one task depends on another, and then a third. Each step ends up nested inside the previous one.
callbacks.why: Callback hell wasn't just ugly. The real pain was error handling: you had to check for errors separately at every level, and if you missed one, the error vanished silently. Promises were created to solve exactly this.
pros: The simplest idea: no extra concepts needed.
Still the right tool for events.
Lighter than promises, with no microtask overhead.
cons: Nesting pushes the code further to the right at every step.
Errors must be handled at every level.
It's easy to call a callback twice by accident.
gotchas: In Node style, the error comes first: (err, data). Forgetting this is a common mistake.
An error thrown inside a callback is not caught by an outer try/catch.
To convert an old callback API to promises, use util.promisify or wrap it in a new Promise.
terms: A function you hand to someone else to run when the work is done.
Callbacks nested inside callbacks, so the code drifts further right at every step.
where: addEventListener still takes a callback. Promises don't fit here, because an event can fire many times.
The function you pass to map or filter is also a callback (a synchronous one).
Node's older APIs are all callback-based, so you need to recognize the pattern.
callbacks.visualCap: Callback nesting drifts to the right, and every level needs its own error check. A promise chain runs straight down, and a single catch handles every error.

promises.q: How does a Promise work internally? What are its three states?
promises.what:
A Promise is like a receipt. The work isn't finished yet, but you're holding something that says "I'll let you know when it's done".

It has three states: pending (in progress), fulfilled (finished, with a value) and rejected (failed, with an error). Once a promise settles, it stays that way forever.
promises.analogy: A laundry receipt. Your clothes aren't back yet, but you have the receipt. Clothes returned = fulfilled. Clothes lost = rejected. And once the outcome is decided, it can't change.
promises.why: Promises fixed the two biggest problems with callbacks: nesting (the chain runs straight down) and error handling (a single .catch() covers the whole chain).
pros: The chain runs straight down, so the nesting is gone.
A single .catch() handles errors for the whole chain.
Combinators (all, race) make parallel work easy.
cons: Once started, a promise can't be cancelled. You need an AbortController separately.
Forgetting return inside .then silently breaks the chain.
Nothing stops you from nesting promises badly, so you can recreate callback hell.
gotchas: You must return a value inside .then; otherwise the next step receives undefined.
A Promise starts running as soon as it's created. It doesn't wait for .then.
Without a .catch, a rejection becomes an "unhandled rejection", which can crash a Node process.
terms: A container that says "the answer isn't ready yet, but it will be, either a value or an error".
The three states. Once a promise leaves pending, it never changes.
.then() always returns a new promise, which is why chains work.
where: fetch() returns a promise, so every API call relies on this.
It's a thin layer over promises; the same machinery runs underneath.
promises.visualCap: Once a promise leaves pending, it is settled forever. .then builds a chain, and if any step fails, execution jumps straight to .catch.

async-await.q: How does async/await work under the hood? What does await actually do?
async-await.what:
async/await isn't a new mechanism. It's syntax sugar over promises, and the same promises run underneath.

await means "pause here and continue when the result arrives". But it doesn't freeze the whole program. Only the current function pauses, and the rest of your code keeps running.
async-await.why: Promise chains were readable enough, but loops and if-else inside them got awkward. With await, async code looks just like normal synchronous code, and try/catch works the way you'd expect.
pros: Async code reads like synchronous code.
try/catch, loops and if-else all work normally.
Stepping through in the debugger behaves sensibly.
cons: Writing await one after another can make code needlessly slow.
Every async function returns a promise; forget that and you'll end up printing [object Promise].
Top-level await works only in ES modules.
gotchas: Biggest mistake: awaiting things one by one when they could run in parallel. Use Promise.all.
await does not work as intended inside forEach. Use for...of.
If you call an async function without await and it fails, you get an "unhandled rejection".
terms: Makes a function return a promise.
Waits for a promise's result without blocking the thread.
where: Most data fetching today is written this way.
When each step depends on the result of the previous one.

promise-combinators.what: There are four ways to handle many promises together. They differ in just one thing: when the group counts as finished, and what happens if something fails.
promise-combinators.why: Writing await one after another makes work needlessly slow: three API calls that could run in parallel take three times as long. Combinators solve this. And allSettled solves a second problem: if one widget fails, the whole page shouldn't crash.

After a race, the losing request is still running. You need AbortController to actually stop it.

Whichever promise settles first (success or failure) decides the result.
The first promise to succeed wins. Fails only if all of them fail.
where: Several APIs at once: use allSettled so one failure doesn't hide the other widgets.
Use race to put a time limit on a network call.
Use any to take the first mirror that responds successfully.

generators.desc: Functions that can pause and resume using yield. They're the foundation of how async/await works internally.
generators.what:
A normal function runs from start to finish without stopping. A generator (function*) can pause in the middle, at a yield.

The key point is who controls the pause: the caller. Each time you call next(), the generator moves forward.
generators.analogy: A Netflix series. You watch one episode (a yield), then it pauses. Press "next" and the following episode plays. The whole series doesn't play all at once.
generators.why: Generators serve two main purposes: infinite or very large sequences (producing values one at a time without building a full array), and the mechanism behind async/await, which is really generators plus promises, so async/await is built on them.
pros: Lazy: a value is created only when requested, which saves memory.
Infinite sequences are possible.
Key to understanding how async/await works.
cons: The syntax is uncommon, so not everyone on the team will know it.
In most cases async/await is enough.
Debugging is harder because control jumps back and forth.
gotchas: Calling a function* doesn't run its code; it only returns an iterator. The first next() starts it.
With next(value), you can send a value into the generator; it becomes the result of the yield.
Once a generator is finished (done: true), it can't be restarted. Create a new one.
terms: A function that can pause in the middle and later resume from the same point.
The point where the function pauses and hands a value to the caller.
An object with a next() method that returns {value, done}.
where: Process records one at a time without building a full array.
ID generators, Fibonacci: produce only as many values as you ask for.
The whole library is built on generators.

microtask-macrotask.desc: Microtasks (promise callbacks, queueMicrotask) run before the next macrotask (setTimeout, setInterval).
microtask-macrotask.q: What is the difference between microtasks and macrotasks? Predict the output of a tricky async snippet.
microtask-macrotask.what:
There are two separate queues, and the rule fits in one line: run one macrotask, then drain the entire microtask queue, then move on to the next macrotask.

That's why Promise.then always runs before setTimeout(fn, 0), even if the setTimeout is written first.
microtask-macrotask.why: The microtask queue exists so that a promise's result is available before the next paint. Otherwise every .then would arrive a whole frame late and the UI would flicker.
pros: The order of promise callbacks is fixed and predictable.
Microtasks run before paint, so the UI is never shown in a half-updated state.
One mental model explains the whole async ordering.
cons: A chain of microtasks can starve the page.
You have to keep two queues in mind.
Node's model is a bit different (process.nextTick, event loop phases).
gotchas: process.nextTick (Node) runs before other microtasks. It's a separate queue.
To split up heavy work, use setTimeout (a macrotask). Splitting it with microtasks stops the browser from painting.
In an interview, the answer to "what is a microtask?" is: after each macrotask, the entire microtask queue is drained. That one line is enough.
terms: The normal line: setTimeout, setInterval, I/O, UI events.
If microtasks never finish, macrotasks never get to run and the page hangs.
where: Output-order questions are built on exactly this.
Use a microtask to read the DOM right after an update; use requestAnimationFrame for the next frame.
To split a large task, use setTimeout so the browser can paint in between.

prototype-chain.q: Explain the prototype chain. How does property lookup work in JavaScript?
prototype-chain.qsub: What is the difference between __proto__ and prototype?
prototype-chain.what:
Every JavaScript object has a hidden link to its prototype. When you ask for obj.foo and the object doesn't have it, JS follows that link. If it isn't there either, JS goes one level further up, until it reaches null.

This sequence of links is the prototype chain, and it is how inheritance works in JS.
prototype-chain.analogy: If you can't find something at home, you ask a neighbor. If they don't have it, they ask their neighbor, and so on. Eventually you reach a house with no one beyond it (null), and the answer is undefined.
prototype-chain.why: That's why every array has map without it being defined on each one. map lives in one place, Array.prototype, and thousands of arrays share it. That saves memory.
pros: Methods live in one place and are shared by thousands of objects, which saves memory.
Behavior can be added at runtime.
More flexible than class-based inheritance.
cons: Looking up through a long chain is slightly slower.
Modifying built-in prototypes (monkey-patching) is dangerous.
Developers from class-based languages often find it confusing.
gotchas: __proto__ and prototype are different: __proto__ exists on an object, while prototype exists on a function.
for...in also iterates over inherited properties; Object.keys() doesn't.
Don't add your own method to Array.prototype. It will show up on every array and can break libraries.
terms: An object that other objects fall back to when they can't find a property themselves.
An object's link to its prototype.
A property of a function; it becomes the prototype of objects created with new.
where: class uses this chain internally; it's just nicer syntax.
In DevTools, expand [[Prototype]] to see the whole chain.
prototype-chain.visualCap: The lookup moves outward along the chain. map isn't on the array itself but on Array.prototype, and thousands of arrays share that single copy.

class.q: Are JavaScript classes "real" classes? What is happening under the hood?

class.what:
class in JavaScript doesn't add anything fundamentally new. It's the same prototype chain with cleaner syntax.

class Dog { bark(){} } actually creates Dog.prototype.bark.
class.why: The old prototype syntax (Dog.prototype.bark = function...) was scattered, and setting up inheritance took 4-5 lines of boilerplate. class cleaned that up. It also added things that were previously only possible with closures, such as # private fields.

True private fields with #.
Inheritance is straightforward with extends and super.

In JavaScript, plain objects plus functions are often enough.
Deep class hierarchies get heavy quickly.

Class bodies always run in strict mode, even without "use strict".
If you assign a method to a variable, this is lost. Avoid that with arrow class fields (fn = () => {}).

Not new functionality, just a nicer way to write existing behavior.
A truly private field that can't be accessed from outside the class.
where: Keep data and its rules together: validation, computed values.

inheritance.desc: JS uses object-to-object delegation, not class-to-instance copying. extends sets up the prototype chain.
inheritance.q: Explain the difference between prototypal and classical inheritance. When is composition better?
inheritance.what:
In Java, a class is a blueprint and objects are created from it. In JavaScript, an object inherits directly from another object, with no blueprint in between.

class ... extends looks like Java, but underneath it is the same prototype linking.
inheritance.why:
The difference matters because in JavaScript you can change a prototype at runtime and create an object directly from another object, which Java doesn't allow.

The practical advice: avoid deep inheritance in JavaScript. Composition (combining small pieces of behavior) is often the better choice.
pros: The prototype can be changed even at runtime.
You can create an object directly from another object, without a class.
Combines very flexibly with composition.
cons: A deep chain is hard to read and debug.
When the same logic is needed in two unrelated places, composition is the answer.

In an interview, say: "JS has no classical inheritance; it's prototypal with syntax sugar." It's a strong answer.

Class to class, as in Java or C++. JavaScript doesn't have this natively.
Building behavior by combining pieces instead of inheriting.
where: extends Error is the clearest and most common use of inheritance.
React.Component and custom HTML elements require inheritance.

new-keyword.desc: Creates a blank object, sets its prototype, runs the constructor with this, and returns the object.
new-keyword.q: What does the new keyword do, step by step? What happens if a constructor returns an object?
new-keyword.what:
When you call new Foo(), JS does four things, in this order:

1. Creates an empty object.
2. Sets that object's prototype to Foo.prototype.
3. Runs Foo with this set to the new object.
4. Returns the object (unless the function itself returns an object).
new-keyword.why: These four steps matter because many bugs can be traced back to them. Forgetting new breaks this, the prototype link comes from step 2, and what happens when a constructor returns an object is covered by step 4. Interviewers ask this directly.
pros: One consistent, standard way to create objects.
The prototype is linked automatically.
You can detect incorrect usage with new.target.
cons: Forgetting new silently creates bugs (in non-strict mode).
Returning an object from a constructor changes the behavior, which is confusing.
It doesn't work with arrow functions at all.
gotchas: If the constructor returns an object, that object replaces this. If it returns a primitive, the return value is ignored.
Calling a class without new always throws an error. A plain constructor function would just run silently.
You can't use new on an arrow function, because it has no prototype.
terms: Runs a function as a constructor and creates a new object.
where: Classes and constructor functions are both invoked with new.

mixins.q: What is a mixin in JavaScript? How does it address the diamond problem of multiple inheritance?
mixins.what:
In JS, a class can have only one parent. But you often need behavior from two or three places.

A mixin is the workaround: keep the behavior in a plain object or function, and mix it into whatever needs it.

Combinations are cheap, with no new class needed.
Small, separate pieces are easier to test.

garbage-collection.what:
In JS you don't free memory yourself; the engine does it. Its rule is simple: any object that is no longer reachable gets cleaned up.

memory-leaks.q: What are the most common memory leak patterns? How do you detect and fix them?
memory-leaks.what:
A leak doesn't mean "memory is full". It means something is holding on to data you no longer need.

In JavaScript there are only four major causes, and all four are easy to recognize.
memory-leaks.why: This is the biggest issue in SPAs. The page never reloads, so every screen change leaks a little more, and after an hour the app gets slow or crashes.

DevTools show them clearly (heap snapshot comparison).
WeakMap and AbortController fix many of them automatically.
cons: No error is reported; the app just gets slower.
Tracking them down takes time.

Date is widely considered one of JavaScript's worst designs: months start at 0, it is mutable, and its timezone behavior is odd.

The modern approach is formatting with Intl, calculations with a library (date-fns or Day.js), and eventually Temporal.
date-time.why: Date bugs appear silently: a date showing a day early, or the wrong month. So the practical rules are: display with Intl, calculate with a library, and always use ISO strings on the server.

ISO strings remove timezone ambiguity.

try-catch.desc: try/catch/finally is JS error handling. A catch block receives the error object, and finally always runs (even after a return). Uncaught errors propagate up the call stack, and throw can re-throw an error or throw a new one.
try-catch.qsub: What is the difference between throw new Error() and just throw? When would you re-throw?
try-catch.what:
When a throw happens, the function stops right there and the error climbs upward to the caller. If the caller has no catch, it keeps going up. If nothing catches it, the program crashes.

finally always runs, whether or not an error occurred, and even after a return.
try-catch.why: finally is the right place for cleanup, such as stopping a loader, closing a connection, or releasing a lock. It runs on every path: normal execution, an error, or an early return.
pros: Error handling lives in one place, with no need to check after every call.
finally guarantees cleanup.
Errors propagate upward automatically, so intermediate functions don’t need to do anything.
cons: It doesn’t catch errors thrown inside async callbacks.

map-set.q: What is the difference between a Map and a plain object? When would you use a Set instead of an array?
map-set.qsub: What is the difference between WeakMap and Map? Why can't you enumerate WeakMap keys?
map-set.what:
An object also stores key-value pairs, so why do we need Map?

Three reasons: a Map's keys can be anything (objects, functions), it keeps insertion order, and it gives you .size directly. It is also fast at adding and deleting entries in large collections.
map-set.why: Objects were never designed as key-value stores. That is why integer-like keys get sorted, keys can leak in from the prototype, and keys are limited to strings and symbols.Map and Set were built for exactly this job, so they are the better tool for it.

For small, fixed data, a plain object is still simpler.
gotchas: JSON.stringify(new Map()) returns "{}", so your data disappears. Convert with [...map] before serializing.
A Set compares objects by reference, so new Set([{a:1},{a:1}]) has a size of 2.
In an object, integer-like keys are sorted automatically. Use a Map if insertion order matters.

weakmap-weakset.qsub: How would you use a WeakMap to implement private class data? What are the limitations of WeakMap?
weakmap-weakset.what:
A normal Map holds strong references to its keys. If a key is a DOM node that gets removed from the page, it stays in memory anyway, because the Map is still holding it.

WeakMap holds its keys weakly. Once nothing else can reach an object, both the object and its entry are garbage-collected.
weakmap-weakset.why: When the key's lifetime is not under your control (DOM nodes, user objects, third-party objects), WeakMap is the right choice. You don't have to write any cleanup code.
pros: Leaks are prevented automatically, with no cleanup code.
The safest option for metadata on DOM nodes and objects.
Also safe to use with third-party objects.
cons: You can't iterate it, and there's no size.
Keys must be objects.
Hard to debug, since you can't inspect the contents.
gotchas: Keys must be objects. Using a string or number throws a TypeError.
Not being iterable is intentional. Otherwise garbage-collection timing would become observable.
Selection rule: do you control the key's lifetime? Yes → Map. No → WeakMap.
terms: Holds keys weakly, so the garbage collector can reclaim them.
A collection that doesn't cause memory leaks.
